column1: # Population-level context for haplogroups. Matched by prefix against the caller's labels
# (Y: ISOGG 2016 long form as emitted by yhaplo, and the short SNP form; MT: PhyloTree 17 name).
# Keep entries short, hedged, and about populations, never individuals.

column5: text
The deepest branches of the human Y tree, found mainly in Southern and Eastern Africa (Khoisan, Ethiopian and Sudanese groups).
An old African lineage, most common among Central African hunter-gatherer groups and in East Africa.
Spread across Asia, Oceania and the Americas: C-M217 is common in Mongolia, Siberia and East Asia; C-M38 in New Guinea and Melanesia; C-M130 branches reach Australia.
Found mainly in Japan (D-M55, including Ainu), Tibet and the Andaman Islands.
The dominant African paternal lineage, with branches that also spread into the Near East and around the Mediterranean.
The lineage carried by the Bantu expansion: the majority Y lineage across West, Central and Southern Africa and in the African diaspora.
Originated in East Africa and spread to North Africa, the Near East and Southern Europe; a major lineage in Ethiopia, Somalia, the Maghreb, Greece and the Balkans.
Common from Egypt and Sudan through the Balkans and Southern Europe; E-V13 is a signature Balkan branch.
The characteristic Berber lineage of the Maghreb, also present in Iberia.

A Near-Eastern and East-Mediterranean branch: frequent in Ethiopia, the Levant, Anatolia and Arabia, a well-known component (around a tenth) of Ashkenazi, Sephardic and Mizrahi Jewish paternal lineages, and present at low frequency in Italy, Iberia and the Balkans.

The main sub-branch of E-M34 (YFull: E-M84). Frequent in Ethiopia and Eritrea, the Levant, Arabia and Anatolia; one of the characteristic lineages of Jewish communities from all three main diasporas; sporadic in Southern Europe.

The main sub-branch of E-M34. Frequent in Ethiopia and Eritrea, the Levant, Arabia and Anatolia; one of the characteristic lineages of Jewish communities from all three main diasporas; sporadic in Southern Europe.
A branch within E-M84 (FamilyTreeDNA naming), found in the Levant, Arabia and among Jewish lineages.
Peaks in the Caucasus and Anatolia; carried by early Neolithic farmers into Europe (the Tyrolean Iceman was G2a), today scattered at low frequency across Europe and the Near East.
Mostly South Asian; H1a1 is the main lineage of the Roma, reflecting their Indian origin.
A European lineage present since the Palaeolithic, with little presence outside Europe.
Concentrated in Scandinavia and Germanic-speaking regions; strongly associated with Norse and Anglo-Saxon migrations.
I2a1 peaks in the Balkans and Sardinia; I2a2 is found across Northwest Europe including Germany, Britain and Ireland.
Originated in the Near East and spread with Neolithic farming and later movements across the Mediterranean, Caucasus and South Asia.
Most frequent in Arabia, the Levant and the Caucasus (Dagestan); the J-P58 branch is associated with Semitic-speaking populations.
Peaks in the Fertile Crescent, Anatolia, the Caucasus and Iran; common around the Mediterranean (Italy, Greece, Balkans) and in South Asia.
Mainly South Asian, especially Pakistan and western India, with pockets in the Near East.
Spread from Siberia westward with Uralic speakers; the main lineage in Finland, the Baltic states and northern Russia.
The dominant lineage of East and Southeast Asia: O-M122 (Han Chinese and neighbours), O-M119 (coastal China, Taiwan, Austronesians), O-M95 (Southeast Asia).
Siberian in origin; Q-M3 is the principal Native American paternal lineage, and other branches are found in Siberia and Central Asia.
A widespread Eurasian lineage whose main branches dominate Europe, Central Asia and South Asia.
Most common in Eastern Europe (Poland, Russia, Ukraine), Central Asia and northern India; associated with Bronze Age steppe migrations.
The most common paternal lineage in Western Europe (peaking in Ireland, Wales, the Basque Country); the R-V88 branch is found in Central Africa.
The main Western European branch, carried by Bronze Age migrations; R-U106 is typical of Germanic regions, R-P312 and R-L21 of Atlantic Europe, R-U152 of the Alpine region and Italy.
Mainly South Asian.
A scattered lineage with pockets in the Near East, East Africa (Somalia), Sardinia and parts of Iberia.
Among the oldest maternal lineages, concentrated in Southern Africa (Khoisan) and East Africa.
A deep African lineage found mainly in Central and West Africa.
Widespread across Sub-Saharan Africa and the most common maternal lineage among African Americans.
East African in origin and the ancestor of every non-African maternal lineage; also common across Africa.
One of the two founding non-African lineages, now concentrated in South Asia, East Asia and among Native Americans (via branches C and D).
An East Asian and Siberian lineage; D1 and D4h3 are Native American founder lineages.
Found across Siberia, Central Asia and East Asia, and a Native American founder lineage (C1).
The other founding non-African lineage; its branches cover Europe, the Near East, Asia and the Americas.
East Asian and Siberian, and one of the main Native American founder lineages (A2).
East and Southeast Asian; B4 spread with Austronesians to Polynesia and B2 is a Native American founder lineage.
A minor European and Near Eastern lineage at a few percent frequency.
A minor lineage of Europe, the Near East and South Asia.
A rare lineage in Europe and the Near East; the X2a branch is a Native American founder lineage.
A large branch of N whose descendants include most European lineages.
Common in Southeast Asia and southern China.
An old West Eurasian lineage with branches in Europe, the Near East, North Africa and South Asia.
The characteristic lineage of European hunter-gatherers; today most frequent in Finland and the Saami.
Mainly North African (Berber populations) and Iberian.
A branch of U8 common across Europe and the Near East; three K sub-lineages account for about a third of Ashkenazi maternal lines.
The parent of H and V, found across Europe, the Near East and the Caucasus.
The most common maternal lineage in Europe (around 40%), also frequent in the Near East and North Africa; it spread widely after the last Ice Age.
The largest H branch and the most common maternal lineage in Western Europe; it peaks in Iberia and the Basque Country and is also found in North Africa and the Near East.
Found across Europe and the Caucasus; H2a is more frequent in Eastern Europe.
A Western European branch with a peak in Iberia and Western France.
Found across Europe with higher frequency in the Balkans and Central Europe.
Most frequent in the Caucasus and Near East, with a presence in Sardinia.
A sister of H found across Europe, with high frequency among the Saami, in Iberia and the Basque Country.
Spread from the Near East into Europe with Neolithic farmers; around a tenth of Europeans, higher in the Near East.
The main European J branch (J1c is the most common form in Europe).
Found around the Mediterranean and the Near East.
A Near Eastern and European lineage at about a tenth of the population in parts of Europe; associated with early farming and pastoralism.
The more common T branch in Europe, especially Northern and Central Europe.
Includes N1b, common among Ashkenazi Jews, and N1a, carried by early Neolithic farmers into Europe.
Mainly East Asian and Siberian, including Japan and Kamchatka.
Found in Siberia, Central Asia and among the Saami.
Found in New Guinea and Melanesia.
Found in Australia and New Guinea.
